introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.summary: Tachyon is a polyglot, file-system-routed full-stack framework distributed through the standalone ty binary. Tac is the frontend layer and Yon is the backend/runtime layer.

sections.heading: Install
sections.body: The fail-closed installer downloads and verifies only the standalone `ty` binary; it does not install companion-language runtimes or native platform toolchains. ty doctor reports the additional tools the current project needs. Scaffold an app and start the shape-aware server: Tachyon detects whether your app has a client/, a server/, or both, and serves the right thing on one port.
sections.code:
curl -fsSL https://tachyon.del.ma/install.sh | sh
ty init my-app --name "My App"
cd my-app
ty serve

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: Pages live in client/pages and backend routes in server/routes. Yon also defines services, repositories, clients and delegates as mandatory annotated layers. Optional root middleware uses a Yon language; .tachyonrc retains only bounded worker schedules.
sections.code:
client/
  pages/tac.html
  components/hero/tac.html
server/
  routes/posts/yon.py
  services/
  repositories/
  clients/
  delegates/
middleware.py
.tachyonrc  # workers only

routing.title: Routing
routing.summary: Both layers route from the file system: a directory is a path, and dynamic segments use _slug directories that become :slug parameters at runtime.

sections.heading: Frontend pages
sections.body: client/pages/tac.html serves /, client/pages/docs/tac.html serves /docs, and client/pages/docs/_topic/tac.html serves /docs/:topic — the page you are reading uses exactly that dynamic segment. An ancestor page containing a slot element becomes a reusable shell for its descendants.
sections.code:
client/pages/
  tac.html          -> /
  docs/tac.html     -> /docs (shell with <slot />)
  docs/_topic/
    tac.html        -> /docs/:topic

sections.heading: Backend routes
sections.body: A route file at server/routes/<path>/yon.<ext> declares @Controller on a Controller-suffixed class whose static methods are HTTP verbs. The legacy Handler fallback is removed.

sections.heading: Handler protocol
sections.body: Yon owns JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Kotlin, PHP and Rust runtimes. Other programs are reached from a method on an @Delegate class carrying @Relay; interpreter registration, shebang handlers and executable-handler fallback are removed.

yon.title: Yon backend
yon.summary: Yon is Tachyon's backend/runtime layer: filesystem-routed handlers, one supervised process protocol, middleware, scheduled workers and durable SSE topic logs.

sections.heading: Serve modes
sections.body: ty serve is shape-aware. A client/ app serves frontend assets, a server/ app serves backend routes, and a client/ + server/ app runs full-stack.
sections.code:
ty serve
YON_PORT=8000 ty serve
YON_HOST=0.0.0.0 ty serve --allow-non-loopback
NODE_ENV=production ty serve

sections.heading: Route convention
sections.body: Backend routes live at server/routes/<path>/yon.<ext>. A mandatory @Controller class exposes static HTTP methods; dynamic _name folders arrive in request.parameters.

sections.heading: Languages
sections.body: Routes, middleware and workers use JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Kotlin, PHP or Rust. Keep Ruby, Go, Swift, Zig and other existing programs behind an explicit @Delegate + @Relay edge.

sections.heading: Layers and streams
sections.body: @Controller, @Service, @Repository, @Client and @Delegate must match their server directory and class suffix. @Stream marks a yielding route in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Kotlin or C#; Java and Rust return one response. TY2008–TY2015 report layer and stream contract violations.

sections.heading: Runtime overrides
sections.body: Operators may select the JavaScript and Python executables with YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME and YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME. Removed TACHYON_* names are not aliases.
sections.code:
YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME=/opt/bun/bin/bun ty serve
YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME=/opt/python/bin/python3 ty serve

sections.heading: Process lifecycle
sections.body: Yon invokes one bounded process per request. The current server policy enforces a 30-second invocation deadline and a 1 MiB request-body limit, captures bounded diagnostics, and terminates a child that outlives its request. These limits are built in and are not environment-configurable.
sections.code: ty serve

sections.heading: Protocol response
sections.body: A handler returns a status, headers and body through Handler Protocol v1. Ordinary values become JSON. An explicit text/html response is passed through unchanged; Yon never renders templates and yon.html is rejected.

sections.heading: Specification boundary
sections.body: The Rust rewrite does not generate OpenAPI or host /api-docs. Generate a specification in your application pipeline or keep the legacy server for those endpoints; ty migrate check reports this difference.
sections.code: ty migrate check .

sections.heading: Realtime topics
sections.body: A topic is a bounded append-only NDJSON log under .tachyon/topics. Admission is 128 subscribers globally, 32 per topic and 32 active topics. Tachyon retains 256 replay records, limits each record to 64 KiB and each log to 16 MiB. A cursor-less EventSource starts at the oldest retained replay record; browser reconnection sends Last-Event-ID and resumes at the following record. An explicitly stale cursor closes with topic-error. Capacity exhaustion is HTTP 503: close and retry with bounded backoff.

sections.heading: Security and middleware
sections.body: The server binds loopback by default, rejects traversal, applies security headers and bounds requests and child processes. Root middleware can answer before a route or merge and replace responses afterward. Invocation failures return a redacted x-tachyon-request-id that matches the structured server failure event, allowing correlation without exposing child diagnostics.
sections.code: ty serve

sections.heading: Polyglot middleware
sections.body: Middleware uses the same supervised protocol as routes and must use one of the eight Yon languages. A 204 continues; another status answers early in before or replaces the response in after.
sections.code:
middleware.py
server/
  routes/
    items/yon.py

sections.heading: Middleware phases
sections.body: The before phase receives request metadata and can continue or answer early. The after phase also receives response metadata and can merge headers or replace the response. A failed after hook preserves the original response.
sections.code:
{ "phase": "before", "request": {}, "context": {} }
{ "phase": "after", "request": {}, "response": {}, "context": {} }

sections.heading: External policy engines
sections.body: Raw arbitrary-language middleware was removed. Put the middleware entry point in a Yon language and call an existing policy engine from a supervised @Delegate + @Relay boundary.

sections.heading: Middleware envelopes
sections.body: Process middleware receives metadata-only envelopes so it cannot accidentally consume request bodies or break streaming responses. A 204 result continues or merges headers; any other status becomes the response.

sections.heading: Telemetry boundary
sections.body: The Rust rewrite does not emit OpenTelemetry spans. Instrument at your deployment boundary or keep the legacy server when emitted spans are a migration requirement; ty migrate check reports the difference.
sections.code: ty migrate check .

templates.title: Tac templates
templates.summary: Templates are HTML compiled into client render plans with braces for interpolation, on:event attributes for delegated events, loop, logic, and switch elements for control flow, plus explicit companion mount schedules.

sections.heading: Interpolation and events
sections.body: Braces use a bounded expression grammar with contextual escaping; authored source is never evaluated as JavaScript. Values resolve in the browser from public render-plan state and mounted component companions. Event bindings compile to structured data for one delegated listener per event type.
sections.code: {headline}

sections.heading: Control flow
sections.body: Loops, conditionals and switches are elements, so structure stays visible in the markup. Nested loops use lexical scope: parent bindings remain available in nested iterables, text, dynamic attributes, conditions, component props and event arguments. The nearest repeated loop name shadows its parent only inside that loop, and siblings restore the outer scope. A component owns the evaluated props it receives rather than inheriting the caller's loop scope.
sections.code:
Working…

Done.

sections.heading: Components
sections.body: A component folder under client/components maps to a hyphenated tag: components/panel/users becomes panel-users. Props pass as attributes, and mount="visible" activates the browser-created component when it approaches the viewport. The legacy hydrate spelling remains a mount-schedule alias, not SSR hydration.

sections.heading: Client mount schedules
sections.body: The Tac browser renderer creates every component subtree from the compiled render plan, then activates its companion according to the selected schedule. Use load for immediate activation, idle for background work, visible for viewport-driven activation, interaction for the first user intent, or never for markup with no companion instance. Repeated components, including components inside loops, receive independent identities.
sections.code:
<product-card :product="product" hydrate="visible" />
<cart-summary hydrate="interaction" />
<legal-notice hydrate="never" />

sections.heading: Mount contracts
sections.body: mount must be one of load, idle, visible, interaction, or never as a static literal. The compatibility hydrate spelling has the same schedules. Props must be JSON-serializable public data; never put secrets or authorization state in the client render plan. A failed activation is marked on the browser-created component and can retry on a later interaction.

native-rendering.title: Native HTML rendering
native-rendering.summary: Non-web Tac bundles keep HTML as the only application-facing view language, render supported semantics with native controls, and isolate only unmapped subtrees in local WebViews.

sections.heading: Native by default
sections.body: web remains a browser target. The macos, windows, linux, ios, and android outputs are native-first. The compiler emits Native UI v1 documents, and each generated host applies the bounded state, bindings, and actions represented by that contract. The compatibility controller artifact is DOM-free, but the current hosts do not embed QuickJS or JavaScriptCore controllers.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target macos
ty bundle --target android
ty bundle --target windows

sections.heading: One HTML source
sections.body: Application developers still write tac.html. Before native tree creation, Tac lowers loop, logic, switch and case control elements, resolves Tac components, evaluates bindings, and removes nonvisual script, style, template, and noscript elements. Native hosts map the resulting semantic tree to SwiftUI over Apple platform controls, Android platform Views, Win32 common controls, and GTK4.
sections.code:
{title}

Selected: {selected}

sections.heading: Native-first tag handling
sections.body: Control tags and Tac component tags compile away before native output. Supported semantic HTML maps to native controls. On macOS, iOS, Android and Linux, known standard HTML without a native mapping and unmapped Web Components become isolated local WebSurface boundaries. Windows currently renders an accessible placeholder that opens the content externally because embedded WebView2 remains deferred. A genuinely unknown non-HTML tag still fails so typos remain visible. A semantic nativeUIAdapters mapping always wins over fallback.

sections.heading: Live events
sections.body: Generated hosts handle the declarative bindings and increment, toggle, input, and disclosure actions represented in Native UI v1. The DOM-free compatibility controller is qualified independently; the current native hosts do not execute it and do not embed QuickJS or JavaScriptCore.

sections.heading: Automatic local boundary
sections.body: The compiler keeps supported parents and siblings native while selecting the nearest unmapped subtree as a WebSurface. macOS and iOS use WKWebView, Android uses Android WebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK with generated local resources and no native bridge. Windows keeps the boundary in Native UI v1 but presents an accessible external-browser placeholder until WebView2 passes its viability gate. No app-wide mode or fallback declaration is required.

sections.heading: Remote WebSurface boundary
sections.body: An HTTPS iframe with an accessible name lowers to a remote WebSurface whose bridge is always none. Apple platforms, Android and Linux keep navigation on the declared HTTPS origin; Windows presents the external-content placeholder instead of embedding a browser. The contentSurface, appWindow, shortcuts, screen-capture, camera, microphone, raw-filesystem and shell names in compatibility type surfaces are contracts only in this rewrite and are not implemented device operations.
sections.code:
<iframe src="https://example.com/help" aria-label="Hosted help"></iframe>

# Inspect the emitted boundary and its bridge: none declaration
ty bundle --target linux --skip-package

companions.title: Companions
companions.summary: A tac.js or tac.ts file beside a component becomes its browser-side instance; bounded fields and methods remain explicit.

sections.heading: Component fields
sections.body: The compiler serializes bounded expression trees without evaluating them. The Tac browser renderer resolves fields, methods, structure and dynamic attributes against the owning component instance and rerenders after event handlers run.

sections.heading: Browser lifecycle and storage
sections.body: The companion mount lifecycle runs after the browser creates the component subtree. The legacy hydrate(root, signal) method remains a compatibility hook. Use standards such as sessionStorage, localStorage and CustomEvent directly; the AbortSignal gives listeners and asynchronous work a deterministic teardown boundary.

polyglot.title: Polyglot companions
polyglot.summary: Component companions can be compiled by real native-language toolchains and exposed to browser islands through one bounded ABI.

sections.heading: Choose a companion language
sections.body: A browser component may use tac.js, tac.ts, tac.dart, tac.rs, tac.kt, tac.swift, or tac.cs beside tac.html. JavaScript and TypeScript emit modules; Rust, Dart, Kotlin, Swift and C# are compiled by rustc, dart, kotlinc-js, swiftc and dotnet rather than by a Tachyon language subset.
sections.code:
client/components/counter/
  tac.html
  tac.swift

var count = 6
func doubled() -> Int { count * 2 }
let tac: [String: TacMember] = [
  "count": .field({ count }, { count = $0 as? Int ?? count }),
  "doubled": .method({ _ in doubled() }),
]

sections.heading: Declare the ABI
sections.body: A native-language companion declares the readable fields, writable fields and callable methods its island may reach. The host exposes those members through get, set and call operations, so it never guesses from reflection and never evaluates companion source.

sections.heading: Contracts stay on the server
sections.body: The Rust runtime does not discover or enforce legacy OPTIONS.schema.json request and response contracts. Validate at the handler or deployment boundary; ty migrate check reports each legacy route schema as unsupported with an explicit action. Browser companions use normal browser HTTP APIs rather than declaring a second route protocol.

sections.heading: Toolchain boundary
sections.body: The WebAssembly ABI intentionally exposes data and methods, not an implicit browser or native SDK. Keep browser APIs in JavaScript or TypeScript islands and keep native host capabilities behind the generated platform controller. A missing toolchain fails the build with ty doctor guidance.
sections.code:
ty doctor
ty build

# Native-language browser companions require matching compilers:
# rustc, dart, kotlinc-js, swiftc + WebAssembly SDK, or dotnet

devices.title: Devices and targets
devices.summary: Tac builds one client source tree into a browser output or native desktop and mobile controls. The rooted terminology: platform is the form factor (desktop/mobile/web); environment and os are synonyms for the concrete host (windows/macos/linux/android/ios/web); target is the bundle output.

sections.heading: Targets
sections.body: The accepted bundle targets are web, macos, windows, linux, ios and android. web emits browser assets; every non-web target uses the native renderer by default. The all target expands to every available target and writes sibling directories under dist/. Accepted names describe CLI availability, not a shared support tier.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target web      # dist/web
ty bundle --target macos    # dist/macos
ty bundle --target windows  # dist/windows
ty bundle --target linux    # dist/linux
ty bundle --target ios      # dist/ios
ty bundle --target android  # dist/android
ty bundle --target all

sections.heading: One native-first policy
sections.body: Every non-web target maps known Tac HTML semantics to platform controls and preserves native siblings when an unmapped subtree appears. macOS and iOS use WKWebView for that local boundary, Android uses Android WebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. Windows has no embedded WebView and emits an accessible placeholder that opens the content externally. The former render-mode flag and TAC_RENDER_MODE override have been removed.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target macos    # SwiftUI + inferred WKWebView boundaries
ty bundle --target android  # Android Views + inferred WebView boundaries
ty bundle --target windows  # Win32 controls + external placeholder

sections.heading: Preview
sections.body: Preview accepts exactly one target. If you omit --target, Tachyon previews web. Native previews run prerequisite checks first so missing Xcode or Swift, the Android SDK, Windows build tools, GTK, or a local-WebSurface dependency used by Apple, Android or Linux fails early with an actionable message.
sections.code:
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos
ty preview --target android

sections.heading: Runtime globals
sections.body: Templates can read platform, environment, os and target without imports. Every companion language can read the same structured context through its Tac runtime binding.
sections.code:
<switch :value="platform">
  <case :when="'desktop'">Desktop bundle on {os}</case>
  <case :when="'mobile'">Mobile bundle on {os}</case>
  <case default>Web platform</case>
</switch>

const platform = this.tac.platform.platform  // desktop | mobile | web
const os = this.tac.platform.os              // windows | macos | linux | android | ios | web

sections.heading: Rooted terminology
sections.body: platform is the form factor: macos, windows and linux targets are the desktop platform; ios and android are the mobile platform; web is the web platform. environment and os are synonyms for the concrete host: the operating system for native bundles, web for browser bundles (the detected visitor OS stays on browserOS). target names the bundle output. Companion language names the language a Tac companion is written in: JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Rust, Kotlin, Swift or C#.

storage.title: Storage and data
storage.summary: Browser companions use standard storage APIs and Yon streams bounded topic logs over Server-Sent Events.

sections.heading: Browser-local state
sections.body: Browser companions can combine localStorage, IndexedDB, OPFS, CustomEvent and BroadcastChannel for client-owned state. Tachyon does not add a server database or collection API.

sections.heading: Yon topic logs
sections.body: A Yon application may append NDJSON records to .tachyon/topics/<topic>.jsonl. EventSource subscribers receive each integer position as the event id. Browser auto-reconnection resumes at Last-Event-ID + 1; a new cursor-less source starts at the oldest retained floor. Named topic-error events carry canonical JSON with code, sanitized message, category, guidance and terminal=true; parse the payload and close the source, recreating it without ?position= after TY_TOPIC_CURSOR_STALE. Limits are 128 global subscribers, 32 per topic, 32 active topics, 256 replay records, 64 KiB per record and 16 MiB per log. HTTP 503 means close and retry with bounded backoff. Tachyon does not provide the legacy realtime mailbox or database layer.

cookbook.title: Cookbook
cookbook.summary: Concrete recipes for building Tachyon apps without leaving the frontend-first workflow. This website is frontend-only, so these patterns can be explored with Tac companions before a Yon server exists.

sections.heading: Frontend-only prototype
sections.body: Start with client/ only. Tac renders pages and components, and companions provide the reactive UI controller. When you later add server/routes, the UI contract can stay the same.
sections.code:
client/
  pages/tac.html
  components/panel/users/tac.html
  components/panel/users/tac.kt
  shared/data/docs.json

sections.heading: Event-driven islands
sections.body: Browser CustomEvent provides explicit communication between islands. A form can dispatch a collection change and interested islands can subscribe through their hydrate AbortSignal without knowing who sent it.

sections.heading: Polyglot middleware boundary
sections.body: When the frontend prototype grows a Yon server, add one root middleware.<ext> source in a Yon language. Keep an existing policy engine in another language behind an explicit @Delegate + @Relay boundary.

sections.heading: Native target polish
sections.body: Author semantic HTML once, then bundle web, desktop and mobile outputs. The native planner lowers supported structure into platform controls and isolates only unmapped subtrees in local WebView boundaries.
sections.code:
Workspace

ty bundle --target macos ty bundle --target android

environment.title: Environment variables
environment.summary: A complete inventory of current Tachyon-owned TAC_ and YON_ environment variables, with defaults, precedence, use cases and an explicit scope for the Rust framework and its repository gates.

sections.heading: Naming, support and precedence
sections.body: TAC_ owns client compilation, packaging and repository tooling; YON_ owns server, handler and deployment policy. Command-line flags win over environment variables. Rust rewrite means the current ty binary reads the variable. Internal variables are set by Tachyon itself and are not user configuration. Secret-bearing values must come from a secret manager and must never be committed to .env files.
sections.code:
# Current Rust rewrite
TAC_BUNDLE_TARGET=web ty bundle
YON_PORT=8080 ty serve

# Operator-owned isolation policy
YON_ISOLATION=process ty serve

sections.heading: Current Rust CLI and build
sections.body: These are the supported application-facing overrides read by the greenfield Rust implementation. Empty values are treated as unset where noted; explicit CLI arguments take precedence.

variables.name: TAC_APP_NAME
variables.use: Supplies the name for ty init when --name is omitted.

variables.name: TAC_BUNDLE_TARGET
variables.values: web, macos, windows, linux, android, ios, all; comma/space list
variables.use: Selects bundle targets when --target is absent.

variables.name: TAC_TARGET
variables.values: Same target values; web default where allowed
variables.use: Fallback target selector for bundle and preview; also carries the selected target into a postBundle hook.

variables.name: TAC_PREVIEW_TARGET
variables.use: Selects the artifact served by ty preview when --target is absent.

variables.name: TAC_CACHE_DIR
variables.values: Filesystem path; platform cache by default
variables.use: Moves the Tachyon runtime cache for hermetic builds, CI caches or restricted home directories.

variables.name: TAC_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME
variables.values: Executable path; Node then Bun fallback
variables.use: Chooses the JavaScript executable used for tac.config.js postBundle hooks.

variables.name: TAC_KOTLIN_WASM_STDLIB
variables.use: Lets ty doctor and Kotlin/Wasm companion compilation find the standard library missing from kotlinc-js distributions.

variables.name: YON_HOST
variables.use: Sets the ty serve bind address; non-loopback binding still requires explicit CLI opt-in.

variables.name: YON_HOSTNAME
variables.use: Compatibility fallback bind address when YON_HOST is unset.

variables.name: YON_PORT
variables.use: Sets the ty serve listening port.

variables.name: YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME
variables.use: Selects the JavaScript or TypeScript runtime used by supervised Yon handlers.

variables.name: YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME
variables.values: Executable path; python3 default on Unix and python on Windows
variables.use: Selects the Python runtime used by supervised Yon handlers.

variables.name: TAC_DIST_PATH
variables.values: Filesystem path; dist/web or dist default
variables.use: Overrides bundle output and the directory served by development/native commands.

variables.name: YON_SKIP_BUNDLE
variables.use: Starts ty serve from an existing artifact without its initial bundle step.

sections.heading: Yon process and Firecracker isolation
sections.body: Isolation policy is deployment-owned and has no project-file equivalent. Invalid, partial, non-Unicode or unsafe configuration fails with TY2010 before any handler runs. Firecracker mode delegates Handler Protocol v1 to a separately qualified control program; selecting it does not by itself prove microVM isolation.

variables.name: YON_ISOLATION
variables.use: Selects direct supervised child processes or the Firecracker control-driver boundary for every Yon entry point.

variables.name: YON_FIRECRACKER_DRIVER
variables.values: Absolute executable regular file; required in firecracker mode
variables.use: Names the trusted control program; symlinks and group/world-writable files are rejected.

variables.name: YON_FIRECRACKER_POOL
variables.use: Selects an operator-owned microVM pool without exposing pool choice to application code.

variables.name: YON_FIRECRACKER_VCPUS
variables.use: Requests the bounded vCPU allocation passed to the control program.

variables.name: YON_FIRECRACKER_MEMORY_MIB
variables.use: Requests bounded guest memory in MiB.

variables.name: YON_FIRECRACKER_EGRESS
variables.use: Makes deny-egress explicit; any other value fails closed.

sections.code:
YON_ISOLATION=firecracker \
YON_FIRECRACKER_DRIVER=/usr/local/libexec/ty-firecracker \
YON_FIRECRACKER_POOL=production \
YON_FIRECRACKER_VCPUS=2 \
YON_FIRECRACKER_MEMORY_MIB=512 \
YON_FIRECRACKER_EGRESS=deny \
ty serve

sections.heading: Removed compatibility input
sections.body: This name remains observable only because the Rust CLI rejects it with a migration diagnostic. It is not configuration and must not be used by new projects.

variables.name: TAC_RENDER_MODE
variables.use: Removed. The Rust CLI rejects it because non-web targets are always native-first with subtree WebView fallback.

sections.heading: Repository, release and qualification controls
sections.body: These variables operate Tachyon's own CI, installers and qualification suites. Application deployments should not set them unless they are deliberately running those repository workflows.

variables.name: TAC_AUDITABLE
variables.use: Builds release artifacts through cargo auditable.

variables.name: TAC_BASE_URL
variables.values: Release-download base URL; GitHub latest default
variables.use: Redirects Unix and PowerShell installer downloads for lifecycle tests or mirrors.

variables.name: TAC_BIN
variables.use: Selects the Rust binary used by browser, website and compatibility qualification scripts.

variables.name: TAC_INSTALL_DIR
variables.use: Changes where installers place the ty binary.

variables.name: TAC_LEGACY_BIN
variables.use: Selects the compatibility oracle binary for differential tests.

variables.name: TAC_RELEASE_TARGET
variables.use: Selects the target passed to the release artifact builder.

variables.name: TAC_SOAK_ITERATIONS
variables.use: Controls repeated Rust rebuild iterations in the Phase 7 soak gate.

sections.heading: Framework-internal environment
sections.body: Tachyon sets these values for a bounded child process or at compile time. Setting them manually is unsupported and may corrupt the contract between parent and child.

variables.name: TAC_CONFIG
variables.use: Identifies the configuration module to the isolated postBundle hook runner.

variables.name: TAC_PRODUCT_VERSION
variables.use: Carries the product version from the contracts build script into compiled Rust code.

variables.name: TAC_STAGE
variables.use: Carries the unpublished build root into the postBundle hook runner.

variables.name: YON_HANDLER_PROTOCOL
variables.use: Marks direct handler children as Handler Protocol v1 processes.

sections.heading: External environment conventions
sections.body: Tachyon also honors environment names owned by operating systems and external toolchains. They are intentionally not renamed: NODE_ENV=production disables watch/initial bundling in Rust development serving; HOST and PORT are lower-priority bind fallbacks; CI selects non-interactive repository behavior; HOME, USERPROFILE, LOCALAPPDATA and XDG_CACHE_HOME locate platform caches; PATH locates compilers; ANDROID_HOME and ANDROID_SDK_ROOT locate Android tooling; CARGO_TARGET_DIR and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH control Cargo output and reproducible releases. The compatibility oracle also recognizes DART because that contract belongs to its toolchain, not Tachyon. Prefer TAC_ or YON_ for every variable your Tachyon application itself owns.
sections.code:
NODE_ENV=production YON_PORT=8080 ty serve
ANDROID_SDK_ROOT=/opt/android-sdk ty bundle --target android
SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0 TAC_RELEASE_TARGET=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu scripts/release/build-artifact.sh

operations.title: Operations
operations.summary: Loopback-safe serving, bounded child processes, middleware phases, deterministic builds and stable diagnostics form the operational baseline.

sections.heading: Diagnostics and migration evidence
sections.body: Compiler, server and toolchain failures use stable TY diagnostics with bounded details. Failed Yon invocations return an x-tachyon-request-id that matches the redacted structured server event. Stream delivery admits at most two queued 256 KiB events and 64 MiB total per invocation; a failed stream ends with a sanitized error event carrying the request ID. ty doctor reports companion and project-derived Yon toolchains. ty migrate check records intentional compatibility changes before cutover.

sections.heading: Readiness and signal lifecycle
sections.body: For serve, preview and bundle --watch, parse standard error as one compact JSON event per line. runtime.signal_handlers_ready is handler-registration evidence only; it is not application readiness. Wait for the readiness announcement on standard output and a successful deployment health probe before routing traffic. The first supported signal emits runtime.shutdown_requested and requests graceful shutdown. The development server bounds its owned internal tasks, but preview may await cooperative connection drain and bundle --watch may finish its synchronous fingerprint pass or current bounded build. Supervisors must enforce their own grace period and send a second signal for a hard escape. That second signal emits runtime.shutdown_forced and exits with 130 for Unix SIGINT or Windows CTRL-C, 143 for Unix SIGTERM, or 131 for Windows CTRL-BREAK. Unix SIGKILL, Windows TerminateProcess, out-of-memory termination and host shutdown are not observable. See the full event and privacy contract at docs/SIGNAL_LIFECYCLE.md.
sections.code:
# stderr: parse one JSON object per line
{"event":"runtime.signal_handlers_ready","installed":["SIGINT","SIGTERM"]}
# registration evidence only — now wait for stdout readiness and health
# stdout: Tachyon server ready at http://127.0.0.1:8080/

sections.heading: Build and deploy
sections.body: ty bundle writes dist/web by default. Use --target all during release validation, then preview or package the individual target you intend to ship.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target all
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos

sections.heading: Security
sections.body: Security headers, loopback-only default binding, traversal rejection, request limits and handler deadlines are enforced by the Rust server. Application authentication and API schema generation stay explicit deployment concerns.

sections.heading: Handler cache recovery
sections.body: Compiled Yon artifacts use the project-local .tachyon/handlers cache, confined through non-following directory handles and pruned to 256 recursively accounted entries and 512 MiB. Tachyon reclaims abandoned locks automatically. If manual recovery is necessary, stop every Tachyon process for the project, rename the entire .tachyon/handlers directory on the same filesystem, rerun the command, and retain the backup until the rebuild succeeds. ty cache status and ty cache clean operate on the separate installation/runtime cache selected by TAC_CACHE_DIR; they never repair or delete .tachyon/handlers.
sections.code:
# After stopping every ty process for this project
mv .tachyon/handlers .tachyon/handlers.investigation
ty serve

sections.heading: Rollback
sections.body: Restore the ty binary, Yon handler sources, and .tachyonrc as one versioned unit. A partial rollback can revive removed interpreter registrations, shebang execution, or Handler fallback assumptions and is unsupported.

platform-apis.title: Platform APIs
platform-apis.summary: Browser companions use standard Web APIs directly. Native targets currently expose rendering, declarative state and isolated WebSurface behavior, but no public device-operation bridge.

sections.heading: Current target availability
sections.body: Browser output can use storage, fetch, clipboard, file selection, geolocation, notifications, camera and microphone through standard browser APIs when the user agent and page permissions allow them. Tachyon does not wrap those browser permissions in a separate device bridge.

sections.heading: Current native boundary
sections.body: The generated macOS, iOS, Android, Windows and Linux hosts implement Native UI v1 rendering, bounded declarative interactions, lifecycle records, and bridge-free WebSurface handling where the platform supports embedding. They do not currently implement public contentSurface, appWindow, shortcuts, screenCapture, camera, microphone, raw-filesystem or shell operations. Names for those operations may remain in compatibility type declarations, but they are contracts only and must not be presented as usable host features.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target linux --skip-package
# inspect dist/linux/native-ui and dist/linux/capability-manifest.json

sections.heading: Manifest boundary
sections.body: Artifact Manifest v1 records generated outputs and toolchain evidence, while Capability Manifest v1 is deny-by-default. The legacy-compatible tachyon.host.json may contain a broad hostCapabilities vocabulary; that list is not target-concrete runtime evidence and applications must not treat it as feature detection. A WebSurface's bridge: none field is the enforceable statement for embedded content.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target macos --skip-package
# inspect dist/macos/artifact-manifest.json
# inspect dist/macos/capability-manifest.json
# inspect dist/macos/native-ui/*.json for bridge: none

sections.heading: Companion boundary
sections.body: JavaScript and TypeScript browser companions can use standards-backed browser APIs directly. Native-language WebAssembly companions expose only the fields and methods they declare in their tac member map; no implicit browser API or native device-operation bridge is added to that ABI.

sections.heading: Isolated web surfaces
sections.body: Local fallback and remote WebSurface boundaries never receive a native bridge. macOS and iOS use WKWebView, Android uses Android WebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK; their navigation policies confine local resources and remote origins. Windows has no embedded WebView and opens placeholder content externally on request. Native device adapters, host extensions and biometrics remain unavailable until a target has an audited implementation and native execution evidence.
